Super Contribution Caps 2026-27: Concessional and Non-Concessional Limits Explained

Published: 2 May 2026 · Last updated: 1 June 2026 · By Sarah Mitchell, CFA

From 1 July 2026, two of the most important numbers in Australian superannuation are going up. The concessional contribution cap rises from $30,000 to $32,500, and the non-concessional cap climbs from $120,000 to $130,000. For most Australians, those increases might sound modest — an extra $2,500 and $10,000 respectively. But when you factor in compounding returns inside a low-tax super environment, the long-run impact of maxing out these new caps is significantly larger than the headline numbers suggest.

What Are Super Contribution Caps?

Superannuation in Australia enjoys generous tax treatment: earnings inside super are taxed at just 15%, compared to up to 47% on personal income. To prevent high earners from sheltering unlimited wealth in super, the government limits how much you can contribute each year before extra tax applies. These annual limits are called contribution caps, and they come in two types.

Concessional contributions are contributions made from pre-tax income. They include your employer's Superannuation Guarantee (SG) payments, any salary sacrifice arrangements you have in place, and personal contributions you claim as a tax deduction. They are called "concessional" because you receive a tax concession — the money is taxed at just 15% inside the fund instead of at your marginal rate.

Non-concessional contributions are made from after-tax income. You have already paid income tax on this money, so no tax is deducted when it enters your super fund. However, once inside, it grows in the same low-tax environment.

The New Caps from 1 July 2026

The concessional contribution cap is indexed to Average Weekly Ordinary Time Earnings (AWOTE) in increments of $2,500. Following the December 2025 quarter AWOTE release in February 2026, the ATO confirmed the uplift for the next financial year.

Super contribution caps — FY2025-26 vs FY2026-27
Contribution Type 2025-26 Cap 2026-27 Cap Change
Concessional (pre-tax)$30,000$32,500+$2,500
Non-concessional (after-tax)$120,000$130,000+$10,000
Bring-forward (3-year NCC)$360,000$390,000+$30,000
Transfer Balance Cap$2,000,000$2,100,000+$100,000

These are the caps that apply to contributions made on or after 1 July 2026. Contributions made before 30 June 2026 are assessed against the current-year caps and cannot be retrospectively reassessed under the new limits.

Concessional Contributions in 2026-27

What Counts Toward the $32,500 Cap?

Every concessional contribution your fund receives is counted against your annual cap — regardless of who made it. That means your employer's mandatory 12% SG, any salary sacrifice you have arranged, and any personal after-tax contributions you later claim as a tax deduction all add up toward the same $32,500 limit.

For a full-time employee earning $120,000, the employer SG at 12% comes to $14,400. That leaves $18,100 of cap space for salary sacrifice or personal deductible contributions before hitting the limit. At $180,000, the SG component alone reaches $21,600, leaving $10,900 of headroom.

Tax Benefit of Filling the Concessional Cap

Every dollar of concessional contribution is taxed at 15% inside the fund rather than at your marginal rate. For someone in the 37% income tax bracket (income between $135,001 and $190,000), the effective saving is 22 cents per dollar contributed concessionally. On $32,500 fully contributed: that is a tax saving of approximately $7,150 compared with receiving the same amount as take-home pay.

For individuals earning above $250,000, Division 293 tax applies — an additional 15% on concessional contributions. This brings their effective tax rate inside super to 30%, still lower than the 47% marginal rate but a meaningful consideration when planning contribution levels.

Exceeding the Concessional Cap

Going over $32,500 in concessional contributions in a single year is not catastrophic, but it is expensive. The ATO will issue an excess concessional contributions assessment. The excess amount is included in your assessable income and taxed at your marginal rate, with a 15% offset (to account for the fund-level tax already paid). You can choose to release the excess from your fund to cover the tax bill. If you leave it in the fund, it counts towards your non-concessional cap as well, which could trigger a second excess assessment.

Non-Concessional Contributions in 2026-27

The $130,000 Annual Cap

Non-concessional contributions (NCCs) are a powerful way to move money into the super environment after you have already paid income tax on it. You do not get a tax deduction for making them, but earnings on that money inside super will be taxed at just 15% (or 0% in the pension phase), compounding far more efficiently than in a regular investment account.

From 1 July 2026, the NCC cap rises to $130,000 per year. Eligibility to make NCCs at all depends on your total superannuation balance (TSB) as at 30 June of the previous financial year. If your TSB on 30 June 2026 was $2.1 million or more (the new general transfer balance cap), your NCC cap for 2026-27 is zero.

The Bring-Forward Rule: Up to $390,000 in One Year

One of the most powerful features of the NCC framework is the bring-forward rule. If you are under 75 at any point during the financial year and your TSB is below the relevant threshold, you can bring forward up to three years of NCC caps into a single year. From 1 July 2026, with the cap at $130,000, the maximum three-year bring-forward is $390,000.

Your eligibility tier depends on your TSB at 30 June 2026:

NCC bring-forward eligibility tiers — FY2026-27
TSB on 30 June 2026 Bring-Forward Available Maximum Contribution
Below $1.84 million3 years$390,000
$1.84m to below $1.97m2 years$260,000
$1.97m to below $2.1m1 year only$130,000
$2.1 million or moreNil$0

One important caution: if you already triggered the bring-forward rule in 2024-25 or 2025-26 and are still within your bring-forward period, the increased cap does not automatically apply to your arrangement. The amount available under your bring-forward is locked at the cap that was in place when you first triggered it.

How the Caps Interact With Carry-Forward Contributions

The concessional carry-forward rule allows individuals with a TSB below $500,000 at 30 June of the previous year to use unused concessional cap amounts from the past five financial years. With the 2026-27 cap now at $32,500, the maximum possible carry-forward total in a single year is $175,000 — made up of the current-year $32,500 cap plus unused amounts from financial years 2021-22 through 2025-26.

It is worth noting that unused cap amounts from 2020-21 expired permanently on 30 June 2026. If you had unused amounts from that year, they cannot be recovered. Going forward, 2021-22 unused amounts will be the oldest available in 2026-27.

CalcPhi's dedicated guide on catch-up super contributions walks through the full mechanics with a worked example — highly recommended if you have had years of low or zero contributions due to parental leave, a career break, or reduced earnings.

Worked Example: Making the Most of the New Caps

Priya, 48, earns $160,000 as a senior manager. Her employer contributes 12% SG ($19,200). Her TSB on 30 June 2026 is $420,000 — under the $500,000 carry-forward threshold.

Concessional Contributions in 2026-27

Employer SG: $19,200. Remaining cap space: $32,500 − $19,200 = $13,300. She sets up salary sacrifice of $13,300 for the year. Tax saving at 37% marginal rate: $13,300 × 22% = approximately $2,926.

Non-Concessional Contributions

Priya receives a $100,000 inheritance. Her TSB is well below $1.84 million, so she is eligible for the full three-year bring-forward. She contributes the full $100,000 as an NCC — within the $390,000 bring-forward limit. No tax applies on entry; money now grows at 15% earnings tax inside super.

Net result: Priya moves $113,300 into super in one year, saves nearly $3,000 in income tax, and her retirement corpus is significantly larger than if she had invested the inheritance outside super.

Superannuation Guarantee Rate for 2026-27

The SG rate remains at 12% of ordinary time earnings from 1 July 2026. The maximum super contribution base — the earnings threshold above which employers are not required to pay SG — rises to $270,830 per year, making the maximum mandatory employer SG contribution $32,499.60 annually.

Another significant change from 1 July 2026: employers must pay SG contributions at the same time as wages, within seven business days of each payday. This replaces the old quarterly payment model and means employee super starts compounding sooner.

Age Limits and Work Tests

There is no longer a work test for individuals aged 67 to 74 making non-concessional or salary sacrifice contributions. This was abolished from 1 July 2022. However, individuals aged 75 and over are restricted to accepting only mandated employer contributions — no voluntary or salary sacrifice contributions are permitted once you turn 75, with limited exceptions for downsizer contributions.

The downsizer contribution — allowing eligible homeowners to contribute up to $300,000 per person from the proceeds of selling their principal residence — remains available from age 55 and is not subject to the standard NCC cap.

What You Should Do Before 30 June 2026

A few things close permanently on 30 June 2026. Unused concessional cap amounts from 2020-21 expire on that date with no extension. The current $30,000 concessional cap applies to contributions received by your fund before 30 June — timing matters for personal deductible contributions, where your fund must receive the funds and you must lodge a valid notice of intent to claim a deduction before the deadline. And if your TSB was under $500,000 last 30 June, check how much carry-forward you have available via ATO online services.

Frequently Asked Questions

  • What is the concessional contribution cap for 2026-27?

    The concessional contribution cap is $32,500 for the 2026-27 financial year, up from $30,000 in 2025-26. This cap applies to all before-tax contributions, including employer SG payments, salary sacrifice, and personal contributions claimed as a tax deduction. The increase is driven by AWOTE indexation and takes effect from 1 July 2026.

  • What is the non-concessional contribution cap for 2026-27?

    The non-concessional contribution cap is $130,000 per year from 1 July 2026. If you are under 75 and your total super balance on 30 June 2026 was below $1.84 million, you can trigger the three-year bring-forward rule and contribute up to $390,000 in a single year. Your eligibility and the amount you can bring forward reduces as your TSB approaches $2.1 million.

  • Can I contribute to super if my balance is over $2.1 million?

    Once your total superannuation balance reaches or exceeds the general transfer balance cap — now $2.1 million from 1 July 2026 — your non-concessional cap is zero. You cannot make after-tax contributions. You can still receive employer SG contributions and make concessional contributions, subject to the $32,500 cap and Division 293 tax if applicable.

  • What happens if I exceed the super contribution caps?

    Exceeding the concessional cap triggers an excess concessional contributions assessment from the ATO — the excess is added to your assessable income and taxed at your marginal rate (less a 15% offset). Exceeding the non-concessional cap triggers an excess NCC assessment with a choice to withdraw the excess plus 85% of associated earnings, or leave it in the fund and pay a penalty tax of 47% on the excess. Neither situation is disastrous if caught early, but both are avoidable with proper planning.

  • Does the bring-forward rule apply if I am already mid-way through a bring-forward period?

    If you triggered the bring-forward rule in 2024-25 or 2025-26 and are still within your bring-forward period in 2026-27, the increased cap does not reset or expand your arrangement. The contribution room available to you is still calculated using the cap that applied when you first triggered the rule. The higher $390,000 maximum only applies to new bring-forward arrangements triggered from 1 July 2026 onwards.

  • How does the carry-forward rule work with the new $32,500 cap?

    If your total super balance on 30 June 2026 was under $500,000, you can use unused concessional cap amounts from the past five years on top of the current year's $32,500. The maximum possible catch-up in 2026-27 is $175,000 — that is $32,500 plus up to $142,500 in accumulated unused caps from 2021-22 through 2025-26. Unused amounts from 2020-21 expired permanently on 30 June 2026 and cannot be recovered.
